courseMetadata.title: Performance Across the Stack
courseMetadata.description: Diagnose slow page loads by **measuring before you guess**. Profile end to end, decide whether the bottleneck is backend (query plans, N+1, missing indexes) or frontend (bundle weight, render blocking, unnecessary re-renders), add a cache you can defend, read Core Web Vitals as diagnostics, and finish with a before/after report that survives scrutiny. Hands-on in JavaScript, Python and SQL.

prerequisites.description: Comfortable reading and writing **JavaScript** and **Python**, and writing basic **SQL** joins and aggregates.
Has shipped a web application with a database-backed API and used browser DevTools at least casually.
Familiar with a component-based UI framework (React, Vue, Svelte or similar) at the level of props and state.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: Measurement, localization and reporting are one loop; mixing them stops learners treating baselining as a Section 1 topic.
Caching decisions depend on pricing the underlying query; interleaving forces the 'cache does not fix the query' contrast.
Links each vital to the frontend mechanism that moves it: LCP to delivery, INP to renders.

probeQuestions.prompt: You time a page load ten times. The values in ms are `820, 870, 880, 905, 910, 995, 1020, 1190, 1450, 2340`. Which single line is the most honest summary to put in a ticket?
options: Mean 1138 ms
p50 910 ms, p75 1190 ms, n=10, with the test conditions stated
Best run 820 ms
The last run, since caches were warm by then

optionFeedback.feedback: The mean is higher than seven of the ten runs because one slow run drags it up; it overstates the typical load and hides the slow one.
Right. Percentiles plus n plus conditions is a baseline someone else can reproduce and compare against.
The fastest run is a lucky draw, not a description of what users get.
Warm-cache runs hide the costs real first visits pay; this summarizes your test setup, not your users.

probeQuestions.prompt: Field data for a page shows LCP p75 = 3.9 s (poor-ish), INP p75 = 110 ms (good), CLS = 0.02 (good). Where should you look first?
options: Heavy JavaScript event handlers on the page
Time spent before the largest element could render: server response, a slow API, or blocked critical resources
Layout shifts from images without dimensions
Frontend rendering code, because LCP is a frontend metric

optionFeedback.feedback: If main-thread work were the problem, INP would usually suffer too; good INP argues against it.
Right. Good INP with bad LCP points at pre-render time, which is often on the server.
That is what CLS measures, and CLS is good here.
LCP is recorded by the browser but is often caused by the server; it names what was slow, not where.

routingRules.action: Allow skipping the vitals walkthrough in s1-e3; keep its quiz.

probeQuestions.prompt: A component accounts for 8% of total load time. If you made it infinitely fast, what is the most total load time could improve?
options: About 8%
It depends on how clever the optimization is; it could be much more than 8%
100%, since the component disappears
You cannot tell without a flame graph

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. By Amdahl's law the ceiling on any optimization is the share of total time it occupies.
No speedup of a component can save more time than that component takes.
Only that component's 8% disappears; the other 92% remains.
Share of total is enough to compute the ceiling; a flame graph helps find shares, not this bound.

routingRules.action: Mark Amdahl content in s1-e4 as review.
Recommend the Amdahl runnable example and worked example in s1-e4.

probeQuestions.prompt: A query plan shows `Seq Scan on clinics` for a 40-row table, taking 0.011 ms. What should you do?
options: Add an index on the filtered column
Nothing; a sequential scan is the right plan for a tiny table
Convert the planner cost to milliseconds to check
Rewrite the query so the planner cannot choose a scan

optionFeedback.feedback: On a 40-row table a full scan of one or two pages is cheaper than an index lookup; this plan is already right.
Right. Seq Scan is a fact about the plan, not a verdict. Judge it by selectivity and share of time.
Planner cost is not time; the actual time is already shown.
Forcing an index here would make the query slower.

routingRules.action: Offer the accelerated path through s2-e1.
Recommend s2-e1 in full before s2-e3.

probeQuestions.prompt: A list page issues 1 query for 200 owners, then 1 query per owner for their pets. Each pet query executes in 0.9 ms with a 1.2 ms round trip. What is the best fix?
options: Improve the index on pets.owner_id
Eager-load every association of owners in one big join
Collect the owner IDs and fetch all their pets in one IN query
Nothing; each query is under a millisecond

optionFeedback.feedback: Indexing trims execution time but leaves 200 round trips, about 240 ms of latency.
Loading everything the ORM can reach usually over-fetches massively and can be slower than the bug.
Right. Query count becomes constant in n, which removes the round-trip cost.
The per-query time is not the cost; the number of round trips is.

routingRules.action: Go straight to the s2-e2 code challenge.
Recommend reading s2-e2 before its code challenge.

probeQuestions.prompt: An index exists on `visits (clinic_id, visit_date)`. Which query can use it to narrow its search efficiently?
options: WHERE visit_date >= '2026-09-01'
WHERE clinic_id = 7 AND visit_date >= '2026-09-01'
WHERE cost_cents > 20000
All of them equally; each indexed column is usable on its own

optionFeedback.feedback: The index is ordered by clinic_id first, so a filter on the second column alone has no contiguous range to walk.
Right. It matches the leftmost prefix and then walks a range on the next column.
cost_cents is not in the index.
Column order decides which queries can use a composite index.

routingRules.action: Offer to skim the s2-e3 lecture and start at its faded example.

probeQuestions.prompt: `analytics.js` must run after `core.js` because it calls a function core defines. Which attribute should both script tags use?
options: async
defer
Either; they do the same thing
Neither; always load scripts synchronously

optionFeedback.feedback: async runs each script as soon as it downloads, in any order, so analytics can run before core and throw.
Right. defer downloads in parallel, runs after parsing, and keeps document order.
They differ in execution timing and ordering guarantees.
Synchronous scripts in the head block parsing and delay rendering.

probeQuestions.prompt: A seat map is cached for 60 seconds. Seats are sold continuously. What does the 60-second TTL guarantee?
options: That users always see correct availability
That stale data is served for at most about 60 seconds if nothing else invalidates it
That the underlying slow query no longer matters
Nothing useful; placement is what matters, not TTL

optionFeedback.feedback: TTL does not make data correct; a sold seat can show as free for up to 60 seconds.
Right. TTL is a staleness bound. Correctness comes from invalidating on the write path.
Every miss still pays the full query cost, and misses cluster at expiry.
Placement matters a great deal, but TTL still bounds staleness.

scoringCriteria: Checks field data first to confirm the regression and its size, and which vital moved.
Establishes a lab baseline with pinned conditions and repeated runs, reported as percentiles.
Localizes by share of total (waterfall plus Server-Timing) before hypothesizing a cause.
States a hypothesis together with the measurement that would disprove it.

competencies.title: Measurement discipline and baselining
competencies.description: Establishes a valid baseline before changing anything: chooses the right metric for the question, controls measurement conditions (network, CPU, cache state, data shape), runs enough trials to see variance, and treats a single number as untrustworthy.

desiredOutcomes.description: Produce a reproducible baseline that states the metric, the pinned conditions, n, and percentile spread.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Baseline names cache state, network, CPU and fixture, reports n with p50/p75, and never a single run or a mean as the headline.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: One timing run is a measurement.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Page-load timings are heavy-tailed; a single run can differ from the median by a factor of two, so without variance an 'improvement' may be noise.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the s1-l1 worked example: compute p50 and p75 of ten loads and compare them with any single run from the same list.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Measuring on my dev machine is fine; it is the same code.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A dev machine has warm caches, near-zero latency and a CPU four to six times faster than a median phone, which hides exactly the costs users hit.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: List the four conditions (cache, network, CPU, data shape) and state how your dev setup differs from a median user on each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The average summarizes performance well.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The mean is dragged up by the tail while hiding it; percentiles (p50, p75, p95) describe what users actually experience.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run the percentiles-vs-mean example and note how many samples fall below the mean.

competencies.title: Interpreting Core Web Vitals
competencies.description: Reads LCP, INP and CLS against their thresholds, distinguishes lab from field data, and reasons from each metric to the class of subsystem most likely responsible.

desiredOutcomes.description: Interpret LCP, INP and CLS separately and name the subsystem each one implicates.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correctly rates each vital against thresholds and infers a plausible layer from the pattern, including backend causes of LCP.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Core Web Vitals are a score to raise.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: They are three independent diagnostics of loading, responsiveness and visual stability; a composite hides which one is failing and why.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Revisit the order-tracking vitals example and state what each vital rules in or out on its own.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Lab data and field data should agree; if they don't, the tooling is wrong.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Lab is one synthetic device on one connection; field is a distribution across real hardware and networks. Divergence is information about that diversity.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Write down which question lab data answers and which question field data answers, then explain a 1.2 s lab vs 3.4 s field gap.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: LCP is a frontend metric, so the fix is frontend.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The largest element often waits on a server response or API call; LCP names what was slow, not where the time went.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-read the s1-l3 waterfall: 51% of LCP was one database query reported via Server-Timing.

competencies.title: Localizing a bottleneck to a layer
competencies.description: Reads a network waterfall, Server-Timing headers and a CPU/flame profile together to attribute dominant latency to network, server compute, data access or client rendering, and states the evidence.

desiredOutcomes.description: Attribute the dominant share of load time to a layer, citing share of total, evidence and conditions.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Computes shares that sum to the total, separates waiting from working, and applies Amdahl's ceiling before choosing a fix.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The slowest-looking thing in the profile is the bottleneck.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Wide flame-graph frames often represent waiting, not work; a blocked thread and a busy thread look similar unless you check CPU samples.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Check the CPU-sample view for the wide frame; if it is idle inside, remove or overlap the round trip instead of optimizing code.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Optimizing any slow thing helps.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Amdahl's law bounds the payoff: halving a component that is 8% of total time yields 4%. Localization is about share of total, not absolute duration.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run the Amdahl example and compute the ceiling for each candidate fix before choosing one.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Frontend and backend problems look visibly distinct.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Server time pushes every downstream frontend metric later; without Server-Timing, backend cost is misread as frontend slowness.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Add Server-Timing spans and check whether the server-side split explains the delay the browser reports.

competencies.title: Reading and reasoning about query plans
competencies.description: Interprets EXPLAIN ANALYZE output: identifies the dominant node by self-time, distinguishes estimated from actual rows, and recognizes sequential scans, nested-loop blowups and cardinality misestimates.

desiredOutcomes.description: Name the dominant plan node, its share of execution time, and whether estimates are trustworthy.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Uses self-time and loops rather than cumulative time; treats Seq Scan as a fact to be judged by selectivity; flags large estimate/actual gaps.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A sequential scan means a missing index.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: On small tables or unselective predicates a full scan is the cheaper plan, and the planner choosing it is often correct.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Compute selectivity (rows returned / rows in table) and the node's share of total time before prescribing an index.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Planner cost numbers are milliseconds.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Cost is an arbitrary internal unit for ranking candidate plans; actual time comes only from EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and read 'actual time', ignoring cost when reasoning about duration.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The plan is a property of the query text.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A plan depends on the query plus statistics, data distribution, bound parameters and memory, which is why staging and production diverge.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Analyze plans only against production-shaped data and re-check after statistics refreshes.

competencies.title: Detecting and eliminating N+1 access patterns
competencies.description: Recognizes N+1 patterns in ORM and service-call code from query logs or traces, and restructures the access path so query count is bounded by the schema rather than by result-set size.

desiredOutcomes.description: Rewrite an N+1 access path so the query count is constant in n while the output is unchanged.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Batched rewrite issues a constant number of queries, loads only what the view renders, and preserves output.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Each query is fast, so N+1 is fine.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The cost is round-trip count, not per-query time; 200 queries at 1.2 ms round trip is 240 ms of latency that no index removes.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Estimate count x round-trip time from the query log, then batch the IDs into one IN query.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Eager-loading everything is the fix.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Indiscriminate eager loading replaces N small queries with one enormous over-fetching join that can be several times slower.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Load only what the view renders, in a bounded number of queries; compare rows fetched against rows used.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: N+1 only happens with ORMs.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Loops issuing HTTP calls to an internal service, or correlated subqueries per row, are the same pattern with worse constants.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Scan for any loop containing a network call or per-row subquery and replace it with a batch endpoint or a join.

competencies.title: Designing indexes for a workload
competencies.description: Chooses index columns and their order for a set of queries, reasons about selectivity, covering indexes and leftmost-prefix rules, and states the write-path and storage cost incurred.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a composite index for a stated workload, justify column order, and state the write cost accepted.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Equality columns before range, prefix rule applied to every query in the workload, benefit x frequency weighed against write cost x write rate.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Index every column in the WHERE clause.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Each index adds write amplification and planner choice noise; several single-column indexes rarely substitute for one correctly ordered composite.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: List the workload's queries and design the smallest set of composites that serves them, then count writes per insert.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Composite index column order doesn't matter.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Order decides which query prefixes can use the index at all: (a, b) serves lookups on a, but generally not on b alone.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Check each query against the leftmost-prefix rule and put equality columns before range columns.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Indexes are free reads that cost only disk space.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Every index is maintained on insert, update and delete; write-heavy tables are where over-indexing does real damage.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: State the extra writes per insert and the write rate alongside any index proposal.

competencies.title: Analyzing bundle size and the critical rendering path
competencies.description: Attributes bundle weight to specific modules, classifies each as required-for-first-paint or deferrable, and identifies render-blocking resources and their measurable effect.

desiredOutcomes.description: Classify bundle modules by first-paint need and predict the LCP effect of deferring render-blocking resources.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Distinguishes transfer from parse/execute cost, splits along the first-paint boundary, and chooses defer vs async by dependency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A smaller bundle is always faster.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Parse/compile/execute time and request count matter independently; splitting one bundle into forty dependent chunks can be slower on high-latency links.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Split along the first-paint boundary and re-measure on a high-latency profile rather than maximizing chunk count.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Gzipped size is the cost.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Transfer size drives network time, but uncompressed size drives parse and execution on the main thread, which hurts low-end devices most.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Report both transfer and uncompressed size, and remove or defer code to cut main-thread work.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: async and defer are interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: defer preserves document order and runs after parsing; async runs whenever it lands with no order guarantee, which breaks dependent scripts intermittently.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Use defer for anything with dependencies; reserve async for truly independent scripts.

competencies.title: Diagnosing and eliminating unnecessary re-renders
competencies.description: Instruments a component tree to count and attribute renders, identifies the state or identity change causing them, and removes unnecessary work without altering behavior.

desiredOutcomes.description: Attribute unnecessary renders to their trigger and remove the trigger without changing behavior.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Counts renders, correlates them with a cause, fixes identity or state-commit logic before reaching for memoization.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A re-render is a DOM update.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Most re-renders reconcile to no DOM change; the cost is running component functions, seen in scripting time and INP rather than paint.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Look at scripting time and render counts, not the paint profile, when judging render cost.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Memoize everything.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Memoization has comparison and memory cost and is defeated by unstable prop identity; applied blindly it adds overhead while fixing nothing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Stabilize identities and remove the trigger first; memoize only renders proven necessary-to-skip and expensive.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Re-renders are a frontend-only concern.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Renders triggered by newly fetched but unchanged data are a fetching or cache-invalidation design problem surfacing in the UI.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Compare successive payloads; if data is unchanged, fix the fetch/commit path (version token, conditional request).

competencies.title: Choosing, placing and implementing a cache
competencies.description: Evaluates where a cache belongs for a read/write pattern (client, CDN/HTTP, application, query-result), defines the key, and specifies TTL and invalidation with an explicit staleness bound.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select and justify a cache placement, key, TTL, invalidation path and written staleness bound.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Rejected alternatives named with reasons; key includes every output-changing input and no personal data at shared layers; TTL treated as a safety net behind event-driven invalidation.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Caching is the fix for a slow query.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A cache hides cost on hits and does nothing for misses, cold starts or writes; misses cluster at expiry and peak traffic, so the query still needs fixing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Estimate hit rate and the cost of a miss at peak, and keep the underlying query fix on the roadmap.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: TTL is the invalidation strategy.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: TTL bounds how long data can be wrong; it does not make data right. Without event-driven invalidation a short TTL kills hit rate and a long one serves stale data.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Invalidate on the write path and keep TTL as a safety net; state the staleness bound in writing.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Cache placement barely matters; a hit is a hit.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Layer determines who benefits, what can be invalidated, and whether a personalized response can leak across users.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For each candidate layer, answer: who shares it, can I delete a key on write, could one user's data reach another?

competencies.title: Quantifying and communicating a performance change
competencies.description: Produces a before/after report under matched conditions, reports effect size with variance rather than a best-case delta, attributes improvement to specific changes, and states what was not fixed.

desiredOutcomes.description: Deliver the course project: a before/after report with matched conditions, distributions, attribution, and stated limits.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Meets full-credit rubric on conditions, distributions, attribution, cache justification and honesty.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Before/after is self-evidently causal.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Without matched conditions and one change at a time, the delta may come from cache warming, a quieter network or an unrelated deploy.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Pin conditions on both sides and measure after each change individually.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Report the best result.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Cherry-picking the fastest run inflates the claim and corrupts the baseline the next engineer will compare against.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Report p50/p75 (ideally p95) with n on both sides, never the best run.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Percentage improvement is the headline.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A 60% cut to a 30 ms component is 18 ms and invisible to users; absolute values on a user-facing metric justify the work.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Pair every relative change with the absolute change on a user-facing metric such as LCP or INP p75.

sections.title: Measure Before You Guess: The Diagnostic Loop and Core Web Vitals
sections.description: Build the measurement discipline, the lab/field distinction and the ability to read a trace well enough to say which layer owns the time. Example domain: a **grocery delivery** order-tracking page.

learningObjectives.description: Produce a baseline for a page load that states the metric, the measurement conditions and the variance across repeated trials.
Distinguish lab from field data and state which performance question each is valid for answering.
Interpret LCP, INP and CLS against their thresholds and name the subsystem most likely contributing to each.
Given a network waterfall and Server-Timing data, attribute the dominant share of load time to network, server or client, citing the supporting evidence.
Formulate a falsifiable bottleneck hypothesis and specify the measurement that would disconfirm it.

motivationHooks.prompt: Teams routinely spend a sprint fixing *something* slow, ship it, and see no change, because they never pinned down what "slow" meant numerically. This section is how you stop doing that.
An engineer measures 2.4 s, changes a query, measures 0.9 s and claims a 62% improvement. **Before you start: do you believe it?** Write down yes or no and one reason.
Everything in Sections 2 and 3 (query plans, indexes, bundles, caches) is only meaningful relative to a baseline you trust.

You shouldn't believe it. Two single runs under different cache conditions can't separate a real change from ordinary variance: measured properly, the "62%" was a tail draw and a middle draw from the same distribution.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

A performance number without n, spread and conditions is an anecdote. Core Web Vitals are three separate diagnostics, and LCP is often caused on the server. Attribution is about share of total, backed by Server-Timing evidence, and Amdahl's law caps every fix at its share.
keyTakeaways: Report p50/p75 with n and the four pinned conditions (cache, network, CPU, data shape).
Use field data to size a problem and lab data to diagnose it; divergence is a finding.
LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 at field p75; read each one on its own.
Attribute by share of total with Server-Timing evidence; a fix can never save more than its share.
State every hypothesis alongside the measurement that would disprove it.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

You have almost certainly sat in a meeting where someone said "the site feels slow lately" and someone else said "it's probably the database." Both are guesses, and the second is a guess dressed as a diagnosis. If you act on it you will *find* something slow in the database, because there always is something, fix it, ship it, and the page will still feel slow.

Performance work has a feedback loop that actively misleads you. A test suite tells you plainly whether it passed. A page load gives you a different number every time you ask, and the gap between two runs of *unchanged* code is often larger than the improvement you are trying to detect. Without measurement discipline you cannot tell a real 15% win from a quiet moment on the network, and you will ship both with the same confidence.

This section gives you the instrument before anything to point it at: a baseline someone else can reproduce, Core Web Vitals read as three separate diagnostics, and a waterfall you can attribute to a layer with evidence attached. Sections 2 and 3 assume you can do all three.

## Section objectives

By the end of this section you will be able to:

- Produce a baseline for a page load that states the metric, the measurement conditions and the variance across repeated trials.
- Distinguish lab from field data and say which question each can answer.
- Interpret LCP, INP and CLS against their thresholds and name the subsystem most likely behind each.
- Attribute the dominant share of load time to network, server or client from a waterfall and Server-Timing data.
- State a bottleneck hypothesis together with the measurement that would disprove it.

contentBlocks.title: About the code in this course
contentBlocks.content:
Every example and challenge here runs in your browser, in **JavaScript**, **Python** or **SQL**. JavaScript works offline. The first time you run Python or SQL, the page downloads that runtime (about 10 MB for Python, about 1 MB for SQL), so you need a network connection once; after that it is cached.

Code challenges are meant to be iterated on. Check as often as you like: your score is recorded once, at the first passing check.

## The scene

A grocery delivery company has an order-tracking page that customers refresh while waiting for a driver. Support says it "takes forever." An engineer records ten cold loads of `/orders/48213` on the same throttled phone profile and gets these LCP times in milliseconds:

`820, 1190, 905, 2340, 870, 1020, 880, 1450, 910, 995`

Before any explanation, run the raw data below, then make two predictions about how common code summarizes numbers like these. Commit to an answer first. The value of a prediction is that it can be wrong.

contentBlocks.caption: Ten loads of the same unchanged page. The slowest is almost three times the fastest.

interactionSequence.prompt: This Python program summarizes ten load times, one of which stalled at 9 s. **Predict all three printed lines** before you run it. In particular: is the mean above or below the 8th-smallest value?

codeExercise.code:
timings = [820, 870, 880, 905, 910, 995, 1020, 1190, 1450, 9000]
mean = sum(timings) / len(timings)
mid = len(timings) // 2
median = (timings[mid - 1] + timings[mid]) / 2
print(mean)
print(median)
print(mean > timings[7])
codeExercise.explanation:
The output is `1804.0`, `952.5`, `True`.

Most of us carry a mental picture in which the average sits "in the middle" of the data. That holds for symmetric distributions and fails for the heavy-tailed ones that page loads produce. One stalled run out of ten pulls the mean to 1804 ms, higher than the 8th-smallest value. Nine of the ten users had a *better* experience than "the average," and the one user who had a terrible one is invisible in that number. The median, 952.5 ms, describes the typical case honestly; a p95 would expose the tail. The mean manages to describe neither.

learningExperiences.title: Baselines, variance, and the tyranny of the single run

contentBlocks.content:
## Lecture objectives

- Produce a baseline that states its metric, its measurement conditions and its variance across repeated trials.
- Explain why a mean is the wrong summary for page-load timings, and compute nearest-rank percentiles instead.
- Identify the four measurement conditions that must match before two numbers can be compared.

## The 62% improvement that wasn't

The engineer from the order-tracking scene opens DevTools, sees 2.4 s, changes a database query, reloads, sees 0.9 s, and announces a 62% improvement.

That claim is almost certainly false, and the reason has nothing to do with the query. The engineer took two samples of size one under conditions that differed in at least one uncontrolled way: the second load had a warm HTTP cache, a warm database buffer pool and a warm JIT. Any one of those could explain the whole difference.

A **baseline** is a recorded measurement of current performance, taken under stated conditions, with enough repetitions to show its spread. A baseline is not a number. It is a distribution plus the conditions that produced it.

## Why the mean lies

Page-load timings are **heavy-tailed**: most loads cluster in a band, and a few land far to the right because of a cache miss, a garbage-collection pause, a retried request or a TLS renegotiation. With a long right tail, the mean can sit above most of the samples.

A **nearest-rank percentile** avoids that. For a sample sorted ascending, the pth percentile is the value at index `ceil(p/100 × n) − 1`. The p75 is the value that 75% of loads are at or below.

contentBlocks.caption: Expected output: `n = 10`, `mean = 1138.0`, `p50 = 910`, `p75 = 1190`, `p95 = 2340`. The mean is higher than seven of the ten runs.
Scratch space. Nothing here is graded.

contentBlocks.content:
## The four conditions you must pin

Two performance numbers are comparable only if these match:

1. **Cache state.** Cold or warm, and cold at *which* layer: browser cache, CDN, application cache, database buffer pool. "Cold" is not one thing.
2. **Network profile.** Latency and bandwidth. Latency usually matters more, because most page loads are a chain of round trips rather than one big transfer.
3. **CPU capability.** A developer laptop is roughly four to six times faster than a median phone. Measuring on it hides every main-thread cost you have.
4. **Data shape.** An account with 3 past orders and one with 3,000 take different code paths. Pin the fixture.

## The diagnostic loop

The whole method is five steps, repeated:

1. **Baseline:** measure current state, with variance, under pinned conditions.
2. **Localize:** attribute the dominant share of time to a layer.
3. **Hypothesize:** state what you believe is slow and *what measurement would prove you wrong*.
4. **Change one thing:** one change, so the attribution survives.
5. **Re-measure:** same conditions, same n, and compare distributions, not best cases.

Step 3 is the one people skip. A hypothesis that cannot be disproved is a preference, not a hypothesis.

## An analogy

Timing one page load and calling it "the" load time is like weighing yourself once, straight after a large meal, and calling that your weight. The number is real; it just describes that moment, not you. You would weigh yourself several times, at the same time of day, on the same scale, before claiming a diet worked. Performance baselines deserve the same care: same conditions, several readings, and a summary that is not thrown off by one odd reading.

## Misconception check: "one timing run is a measurement"

This is the most common error in performance work (see misconception `perf-measurement-method-m1`). The 2.4 s and 0.9 s runs above are a draw from the tail and a draw from the middle of the *same* distribution. Measured properly, the improvement they "showed" was zero: the query change may have helped, hurt or done nothing, and the experiment could not tell.

## Summary

- A baseline is a distribution plus conditions, never a single number.
- Page-load timings are heavy-tailed, so the mean can exceed most samples; report p50 and p75 with n.
- Nearest-rank percentile: sort ascending, take index `ceil(p/100 × n) − 1`.
- Pin four conditions before comparing: cache state, network, CPU, data shape.
- The loop is baseline → localize → hypothesize (falsifiably) → change one thing → re-measure.

workedExamples.title: Summarizing ten loads of the order-tracking page
workedExamples.problem: Ten cold loads of `/orders/48213`, same device, same throttled connection, cache cleared between runs. LCP in ms: `820, 1190, 905, 2340, 870, 1020, 880, 1450, 910, 995`. Produce an honest one-line baseline.
steps: **Collect, don't guess.** Ten runs under the same pinned conditions are the raw material.
**Compute the mean:** the sum is 11,380, so the mean is **1138 ms**.
**Compute p50:** `ceil(0.50 × 10) = 5`, index 4, which is **910 ms**.

**Compare.** Seven of the ten runs are below the mean. The 2340 ms run drags the mean up and at the same time hides itself: 1138 says nothing about the one customer in ten who waited over two seconds.
**Compute p75:** `ceil(0.75 × 10) = 8`, index 7, which is **1190 ms**.
workedExamples.conclusion: The honest baseline is: *order-tracking LCP: p50 910 ms, p75 1190 ms, n=10, cold cache, 4× CPU throttle, Slow 4G, 2026-09-20.* The engineer's 2.4 s was a draw from the tail and 0.9 s a draw from the middle; the measured improvement was zero.

hints: Two cases contain no data at all. Handle them first with an early return, before any arithmetic.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A correct summarizer returns `n` with p50 and p75 from a numerically sorted copy. Adding a `mean` as the headline, or sorting without a comparator, produces a confident number from a misleading or scrambled sample.

interactionSequence.prompt: An engineer measures the order-tracking page once at 2.4 s, changes a database query, measures once at 0.9 s, and reports a 62% improvement. What is the most serious problem with this claim?
options: The second run likely had different cache conditions, and with n=1 on each side the difference is indistinguishable from normal variance.

The engineer should have reported the mean of the two runs instead of the difference.
Load time is the wrong metric; only Core Web Vitals are valid.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right: uncontrolled conditions and no estimate of variance. Either alone invalidates the comparison.
Large wins from a single query change do happen. The problem is how the experiment was run, not the size of the number.
Averaging two untrustworthy samples gives one untrustworthy number. Means do not rescue a bad experiment.
Vitals are useful diagnostics but have no special validity. A well-controlled load-time measurement is a legitimate experiment.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A before/after claim needs matched conditions and enough runs on each side to see the spread. Here both are missing, so the 62% is indistinguishable from one lucky and one unlucky draw.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words, explain to a colleague why the baseline line *"p50 910 ms, p75 1190 ms, n=10, cold cache, 4× CPU, Slow 4G"* is more useful than *"about 1.1 seconds."* Mention at least two of its parts.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer notes that percentiles resist the outlier that distorts a mean; that n tells the reader how much to trust it; and that the conditions make it reproducible, so a later "after" number can be compared fairly. "About 1.1 seconds" is a mean with no n and no conditions: it can't be reproduced or compared.

learningExperiences.title: Lab, field, and the three vitals

contentBlocks.content:
## Lecture objectives

- Distinguish lab from field data and say which question each is valid for answering.
- Interpret LCP, INP and CLS against their thresholds and name the subsystem most likely behind each.
- Explain why lab/field divergence is information rather than a tooling error.

## Two kinds of data for two different questions

**Lab data** (synthetic) is a measurement you produce on demand, on one device, on one simulated connection. DevTools traces and Lighthouse runs are lab data. It answers *"what happens on this page, and why?"* It is reproducible and richly instrumented, but it is a sample of one from a device you chose.

**Field data** (Real User Monitoring, or RUM) is timings collected from real visitors' browsers and aggregated. It answers *"what do our users actually experience?"* It is authoritative about impact and nearly useless for diagnosis, because each value arrives with almost no context.

Use them in order: **field data tells you whether there is a problem and how big it is; lab data tells you what the problem is.**

When they disagree (lab LCP 1.2 s, field p75 LCP 3.4 s) the right reading is not "the tooling is broken." It is "our users' conditions differ from my test conditions in a way I have not modelled." Usually that is device class or network latency; sometimes it is cache state: your lab run warmed the CDN, your users hit a cold edge.

## Three vitals, three diagnostics

These are not a score. They measure three unrelated experiences, and blending them into one number throws away the only useful thing they tell you: which one is failing.

rows: When did the page appear to load?
Whatever the largest element waited on. Often a server response or API call, not a frontend asset.
Does the page respond when I touch it?
Long main-thread tasks: heavy handlers, expensive re-renders, big synchronous work.
Unreserved space: images without dimensions, font swaps, banners injected above content.
contentBlocks.caption: The middle band on each is "needs improvement." Section 3 attacks INP directly.

contentBlocks.content:
## The single most important point

**LCP is measured in the browser but is frequently caused on the server.** It tells you *which element* was slow to appear, not *which layer* made it slow. Keep that sentence in mind for the next experience.

## Summary

- Field data establishes *whether* and *how big*; lab data establishes *what* and *why*.
- Lab/field divergence is a finding about device and network diversity, not a tooling fault.
- LCP ≤ 2.5 s = when the page appeared; INP ≤ 200 ms = responsiveness; CLS ≤ 0.1 = stability.
- Vitals are three separate diagnostics; a combined score destroys their value.
- Good INP with bad LCP points away from main-thread work and toward time spent before rendering.

workedExamples.title: Reading a vitals report for order tracking
workedExamples.problem: Field data, p75, last 28 days, mobile: **LCP 3.9 s** (needs improvement), **INP 110 ms** (good), **CLS 0.02** (good). What does this tell you, and what do you do next?
steps: **Refuse to aggregate.** There is no "overall score" worth computing. Two of three are comfortably good.
**Read the failing metric alone.** LCP at 3.9 s is close to poor. INP at 110 ms says the main thread copes once the page is up. CLS at 0.02 says layout is stable.

**Infer the class of cause.** A page with good INP and bad LCP is generally *not* suffering from heavy client-side JavaScript, because that would hurt INP too. Look at time spent *before* rendering: server response, blocked critical resources, or a slow API the largest element depends on.
**Form the hypothesis.** "The LCP element is the delivery-status card, which renders only after `/api/orders/48213/status` returns. I expect that request to account for most of LCP."
**State the disconfirming measurement.** "If TTFB plus that API request is under 600 ms while LCP is 3.9 s, I'm wrong and the time is in asset delivery."
workedExamples.conclusion: The vitals didn't give the answer. They ruled out two large families of cause and pointed at a third, which is exactly what a diagnostic is for. The next experience turns that pointer into an attribution.

fadedVariant.problem: Field p75 for a grocery recipe page: LCP 1.9 s, INP 480 ms, CLS 0.03. Users say tapping "Add all to cart" feels sticky.
givenSteps: LCP 1.9 s is good; CLS 0.03 is good.
INP 480 ms is in "needs improvement," close to poor.

blankedStepAnswers: Main-thread work after load: a heavy click handler or an expensive re-render triggered by the interaction. Loading and layout are fine.

"The Add-all handler updates cart state that re-renders the whole recipe list. I expect a long task over 300 ms on click. If the profile shows no long task on click, the delay is elsewhere (for example, waiting on the network before the UI updates)."

interactionSequence.prompt: Your lab run reports LCP 1.2 s. Field data for the same page reports p75 LCP 3.4 s. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Users' devices and networks differ from the lab profile in a way it doesn't model; the gap is a finding about that diversity.
Field collection is misconfigured, since lab measurement is the more precise instrument.
Report the lab number, because it is reproducible and the field number isn't.
Since LCP appears in both, the cause must be frontend rendering.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Lab is one synthetic device; field is a distribution across real hardware. The gap tells you what your lab setup is missing.
Precise isn't the same as representative. The lab run precisely measures conditions your users don't have.
Reproducibility describes the method, not whether it represents users. The field number is the one describing real experience.
LCP names the element that was slow, not the layer that caused it; it often waits on the server.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Field data answers "how big is the problem for users"; lab data answers "what is happening." When they disagree, find the unmodelled condition (device class, latency, cache state) and add it to your lab profile.

options: True

Right. LCP tells you which element was slow, not which layer made it slow.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: In the next experience's waterfall, 51% of LCP comes from a single database query. LCP is a browser-side symptom with many possible server-side causes.

options: A composite hides which experience is failing, and each vital points at a different subsystem.
It is fine as long as each vital is normalized to 0–100 first.
CLS should be excluded because it is unitless.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Three diagnostics blended into one number lose the only information that directs the fix.
Normalization doesn't restore the lost information: a score of 70 could be any mix of failures.
Being unitless is not the problem; blending unrelated diagnostics is.
Each vital measures a different real experience; dropping two hides responsiveness and stability problems.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Treat LCP, INP and CLS as three separate readings. Report each against its own threshold and ask what each one implicates.

learningExperiences.title: Localizing the bottleneck: waterfalls, Server-Timing and Amdahl

contentBlocks.content:
## Lecture objectives

- Attribute the dominant share of load time to network, server or client from a waterfall and Server-Timing data, citing evidence.
- Distinguish waiting from working in a profile.
- Apply Amdahl's law to decide whether a candidate optimization is worth doing.

## Waiting is not working

In a **flame graph**, width is time on the stack and height is call depth. A wide frame means "this was on the stack a long time." That is not the same as "this used a lot of CPU." A function awaiting a network response is on the stack, wide and prominent, doing nothing. Making its code faster changes nothing.

Before acting on a wide frame, check the profiler's CPU-sample view for work inside it. A frame that is wide in wall-clock time and thin in CPU is a *wait*, and waits are fixed by removing or overlapping the round trip, not by optimizing code.

## Server-Timing: the header that ends the argument

**TTFB** (Time to First Byte) runs from navigation start to the first byte of the document. It contains DNS, connection setup, TLS, request transit, *all server processing*, and response transit.

**Server-Timing** is a response header in which the server reports its own internal timings; the browser shows them next to network timings in the same waterfall:

`Server-Timing: db;dur=412, render;dur=38, cache;desc="miss"`

Without it, all server work appears to the browser as one opaque block, and every downstream frontend metric is simply pushed later. That is why frontend and backend problems do *not* look different from the browser: a slow server makes the frontend numbers worse, and the only way to see through it is for the server to tell you.

contentBlocks.caption: Order-tracking waterfall, throttled mobile, cold cache. API response header: `Server-Timing: db;dur=1890, render;dur=22`.
Amdahl's law as a function. Even an *infinitely* fast connection setup only buys 8.4%.

contentBlocks.content:
## Misconception check: "optimizing any slow thing helps"

It helps, but by how much is capped by **Amdahl's law**: if a component is fraction *f* of total time and you speed it up by factor *s*, total time becomes `(1 − f) + f/s` of the original. The ceiling on any optimization is *f*. A 10× win on 8% of the time is worth 7.2%. This is misconception `bottleneck-localization-m2`, and it is how teams spend a quarter shaving a bundle that could never have moved LCP enough.

## Summary

- Wide flame-graph frames may be waits; check CPU samples before optimizing them.
- Server-Timing makes backend cost visible inside frontend metrics; without it, server slowness looks like frontend slowness.
- Attribute by *share of total*, not absolute duration, and check the shares add up to the total.
- Amdahl: an optimization can never save more than the fraction of total time its component occupies.
- A defensible attribution states the share, the evidence and the conditions.

workedExamples.title: Attributing 3.7 seconds of LCP
workedExamples.problem: Using the waterfall table and `Server-Timing: db;dur=1890, render;dur=22`, attribute LCP to a layer and decide between halving the bundle cost and making the query ten times faster.
steps: **Total the segments.** They are sequential: 310 + 640 + 780 + 1980 = 3710 ms, matching LCP. No unexplained gap, so nothing large is hiding.
**Compute shares.** Connection 8.4%, document 17.3%, JS 21.0%, API call **53.4%**.

**Open the dominant segment.** The API call is 1980 ms and the server reports 1890 ms of it in the database. So 1890 / 3710 ≈ **51% of LCP is one database query**. Network transit for that call is only about 68 ms.
**Test the earlier hypothesis.** It predicted the API call would dominate. It did, and the disconfirming measurement (TTFB + API under 600 ms) didn't occur. The hypothesis survives.

**Price the alternatives with Amdahl.** Halving `app.js`: f = 0.21, s = 2 → 89.5% of original, saving about 390 ms. Query 10× faster: f = 0.51, s = 10 → 54.1% of original, saving about 1700 ms. Instant connection setup: at most 310 ms, whatever you do.
workedExamples.conclusion: The bundle work is real but can't move LCP to "good" alone: its ceiling is 780 ms against a roughly 1,200 ms gap to the 2.5 s target. The query is the only single change with enough headroom. Evidence: *Server-Timing db;dur=1890 against 3710 ms LCP, n=10, cold cache, Slow 4G, 4× CPU.* That is what a defensible attribution looks like, and it is the handoff into Section 2.

fadedVariant.problem: A grocery search results page: LCP 2900 ms. Waterfall: connection 250 ms, document 1450 ms (`Server-Timing: db;dur=1180, template;dur=190`), CSS + JS 900 ms, image 300 ms, all sequential.
blankedStepPrompts: Which segment dominates, and what share of LCP is database time?
What is the Amdahl ceiling if you eliminated CSS + JS entirely?
Write the one-sentence attribution.
blankedStepAnswers: The document request is 1450 / 2900 = 50%; database time is 1180 / 2900 ≈ **40.7%** of LCP.
f = 900 / 2900 ≈ 0.31, so even infinite speed saves at most 31% (900 ms), leaving 2000 ms.
*About 41% of search LCP is database time inside the document request (Server-Timing db;dur=1180 of 2900 ms), measured cold, Slow 4G, 4× CPU; this is the first thing to fix.*

interactionSequence.prompt: Using the order-tracking waterfall, you can either make the bundle twice as fast or make the database query ten times faster this quarter, not both. Which is correct?
options: The query: it is about 51% of total, so 10× takes load to about 54% of today, while the bundle's whole share caps its benefit at 21%.
The bundle, because LCP is a frontend metric and users perceive the frontend.
Either; both are slow, and optimizing any slow component improves total time.
Neither; with 310 ms of connection setup, the network is the real bottleneck.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. That is Amdahl's law applied correctly: the ceiling on a fix is its share of total time.
LCP is observed in the browser but here is mostly caused by server-side database time.
Both help, but not comparably. Share of total decides the payoff.
Connection setup is 8.4% of total, so even removing it entirely caps the win at 8.4%.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compute each candidate's share of total first. The largest achievable saving is bounded by that share, no matter how clever the fix.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In a CPU profile of a slow request handler, one frame is by far the widest. Before acting on it, what should you check?
options: Whether it is consuming CPU samples or merely waiting on I/O.
Whether the function has been optimized before.
Nothing; the widest frame is by definition the bottleneck.
Whether it exceeds one second, since shorter frames aren't worth it.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Wall-clock width and CPU use are different measurements; waits are fixed by removing or overlapping round trips.
Its history doesn't tell you whether the frame represents work now.
Width means time on the stack, which includes blocked time.
Absolute duration is the wrong test; share of the total matters.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A frame that is wide but idle is waiting. Optimizing its code does nothing; eliminating or parallelizing what it waits on does.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **True or false?** If a component takes 8% of total load time, making it ten times faster improves total load time by less than 8%.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. New total = (1 − 0.08) + 0.08/10 = 92.8% of the original, a 7.2% improvement; even infinite speedup caps at 8%.
No speedup of a component can save more time than the component occupies.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Amdahl's ceiling is the component's share. A 10× speedup gets you 90% of that ceiling; infinity gets you all of it and no more.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these measurement setups from **most** to **least** trustworthy for deciding whether a change improved the mobile experience.
options: 20 runs on a throttled mid-tier device profile, cold cache, fixed fixture, reported as p75
Field p75 from RUM over 28 days, compared before and after the deploy
3 runs on a developer laptop, cache cleared, reported as the median
1 run on a developer laptop with a warm cache, reported as the fastest of several attempts

optionFeedback.feedback: Second: controlled and repeated with a representative profile, reproducible and diagnostic, but still one device class.
First: it measures the real user population across real devices, which is exactly the question.
Third: right instincts (cold cache, a median) undermined by n=3 and laptop hardware that hides main-thread cost.
Last: n=1, warm cache and best-of selection combine every measurement error at once.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Field data answers the actual question (did users get faster?). A well-controlled lab run is next best and is what you use to diagnose. Laptop runs hide device cost, and best-of-several with a warm cache measures your luck, not the change.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your ranking?

Why is a wide flame-graph frame not necessarily the bottleneck?
What does Server-Timing make visible that TTFB alone hides?
A component takes 8% of total load time. You make it infinitely fast. By what percentage does total load time improve, and what rule tells you?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: test your measurement code, then transfer it

contentBlocks.content:
## Lab objectives

- Repair a percentile function until a finished test suite passes (lightly scaffolded).
- Write your own test suite that proves a median function correct (unscaffolded).
- Apply the section's ideas to two unfamiliar domains.

contentBlocks.title: The test runner is Jest-compatible, not Jest
contentBlocks.content: JavaScript test exercises run on a **Jest-compatible subset**: `describe`, `it`, `expect` with the common matchers, `beforeEach`/`afterEach` and `jest.fn`. It is not Jest itself: module mocking, snapshot testing and fake timers are not available, so any time-dependent code in this course takes a clock function as a parameter instead. Python test exercises use the standard library's `unittest`.

## Common errors in this section

- **Treating one run as a measurement** (`perf-measurement-method-m1`): always report n and a spread.
- **Measuring on your own machine** (`perf-measurement-method-m2`): pin a representative CPU, network and cold cache.
- **Using the mean** (`perf-measurement-method-m3`): report p50 and p75.
- **Treating vitals as one score** (`core-web-vitals-interpretation-m1`), or **assuming LCP is always frontend** (`core-web-vitals-interpretation-m3`).
- **Optimizing the widest frame or any slow thing** (`bottleneck-localization-m1`, `-m2`): check waiting vs working and compute share of total.
- **Believing backend problems look different from frontend ones** (`bottleneck-localization-m3`): add Server-Timing.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The three bugs: alphabetical in-place sort (copy and pass a comparator), rounding instead of ceiling, and a missing `− 1` that makes p100 read past the end and return `undefined`. sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

A plan tells you exactly where time goes, if you read self-time and not the top line. Seq Scan is judged by selectivity and share, not by its name. N+1 is paid in round trips, so it is fixed by batching, not indexing. An index is a design with a stated benefit and a stated write cost, and column order is the design.
keyTakeaways: Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, read self-time and loops, and ignore cost when reasoning about duration.

Composite indexes: equality columns first, then range; check every query against the leftmost prefix.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

The data layer is where performance problems are both most common and most *fixable*. Common, because almost every request touches it, it sits at the bottom of the stack where costs compound, and its behavior changes with data volume in ways staging never reproduces. Fixable, because the database will tell you exactly what it did if you ask: the query planner shows its reasoning more openly than almost any other component you run.

That combination creates a specific failure. Because plans are readable, developers read them; because they are unfamiliar, they read them *superficially*: spot a sequential scan, add an index, move on. The result is tables carrying fourteen indexes, three of which the planner uses, while every insert pays for all fourteen. The problem was never indexes. It was treating "sequential scan" as a diagnosis when it is a symptom, and never checking share of total time.

Then there is N+1, the most expensive habit in application code precisely because every individual query looks fine. The veterinary clinic's appointment page used in this section was fast for eighteen months and became slow the week a 900-patient practice was onboarded. Nothing changed except *n*.

This section starts where Section 1 ended: the evidence points at the data layer, and now you have to act on it without guessing a second time.

## Section objectives

- Read an `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` plan and identify the node responsible for most of the execution time.
- Predict which of two queries examines more rows and which access method the planner will choose, then check against the plan.
- Detect an N+1 pattern and rewrite the access path so query count doesn't depend on result size.
- Design a composite index for a workload, justify its column order, and state its write cost.
- Split server-side latency into data-access and compute time with instrumentation.

## Lecture objectives (this experience)

- Identify the plan node with the most self-time.
- Tell estimated from actual rows and explain what a large gap implies.
- Explain why planner cost isn't milliseconds and why a sequential scan isn't automatically a defect.

## The schema

A veterinary clinic's practice-management system: roughly 40,000 owners, 61,000 pets and 2.4 million visits.

`owners (id, name, city)` · `pets (id, owner_id, name, species)` · `visits (id, pet_id, clinic_id, visit_date, cost_cents)`

## What EXPLAIN gives you, and what it doesn't

A **query plan** is the sequence of physical operations the database chose: which tables to read, in which order, by which access method, and how to combine them.

`EXPLAIN` shows the plan the optimizer *chose* and its *estimates*. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query and adds the *measured* time and row counts for each node. Estimates come from statistics; actuals come from execution. Only the second is a measurement, and Section 1's discipline applies: run it more than once, because the first run pays for cold buffers.

**Cost is not time.** A cost of `8422.31` is an internal number the planner uses to rank plans against each other. It isn't milliseconds or I/O operations, and comparing costs across databases or configurations is meaningless. The only durations in a plan are `actual time` values, and they only appear with `ANALYZE`.

## Three things to read, in order

1. **Which node added the most time?** Plan timings are cumulative upward: a parent's time includes its children's. Look for **self-time**, the time a node adds beyond its children.
2. **Where do estimated and actual rows diverge badly?** `rows=12` beside `actual rows=48210` means the planner chose on a false premise. Every decision above that node (join order, join algorithm, sort vs hash) was made for a query it thought was 4,000× smaller. Fix the estimate (statistics, a rewritten predicate) and the plan often corrects itself without an index.
3. **How many times did each node run?** A node with `loops=1` costing 40 ms is a 40 ms node. With `loops=900` it is a 36-second node, and that is what a nested-loop blowup looks like from inside the plan.

Sort  (actual time=1840.2..1846.9 rows=3120 loops=1)
  Sort Key: v.visit_date
  ->  Nested Loop  (actual time=0.6..1798.4 rows=3120 loops=1)
        ->  Seq Scan on visits v  (actual time=0.3..1602.1 rows=3120 loops=1)
              Filter: (clinic_id = 7 AND visit_date >= ... AND visit_date < ...)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 2396880
        ->  Index Scan using pets_pkey on pets p  (actual time=0.05..0.05 rows=1 loops=3120)
contentBlocks.caption: Abbreviated `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for the appointment-list query (PostgreSQL output format). Read-only: it is here to be read, not run.

contentBlocks.content:
## When a sequential scan is the right plan

The same page looks up a clinic in a 40-row table: `Seq Scan on clinics (actual time=0.004..0.011 rows=1 loops=1)`. An index here would be *slower*: reading 40 rows from one or two in-memory pages beats walking an index and then fetching the row. A sequential scan is also correct when a predicate is *unselective*: if a query returns 60% of a table, reading it in order beats 60% of a table's worth of random lookups.

**"Seq Scan" is a fact about the plan, not a verdict on it.** The verdict comes from share of total time and **selectivity**, the fraction of rows a predicate matches.

## Why the same query is fast in staging and slow in production

A plan is not a property of the query text. It depends on the query *plus* table statistics, data distribution, the parameter values bound at execution, available memory and which indexes exist. Staging with 8,000 visits and production with 2.4 million legitimately choose different plans for the same SQL, and a production plan can change overnight, with no deploy, when a statistics refresh changes the planner's row estimates. That's Section 1's "pin your data shape" in the data layer: analyze plans against production-shaped data or not at all.

## Misconception check: "a sequential scan means a missing index"

This is `query-plan-analysis-m1`. It leads straight to over-indexing: an index added for a 40-row table, or for a predicate that matches most of the table, makes writes slower and reads no faster. Compute selectivity and the node's share of total time first.

contentBlocks.content:
## Summary

- `EXPLAIN` shows estimates; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` measures. Only the latter gives durations.
- Cost is a comparison unit, not milliseconds.
- Attribute by self-time (subtract children) and check `loops`: a cheap node run 900 times is an expensive node.
- A large estimate/actual gap means everything above that node was decided on a false premise.
- Seq Scan is correct on small tables and unselective predicates; judge it by selectivity and share of time.
- A plan belongs to the query plus statistics, distribution and parameters.

**Attribute by self-time.** The Sort finishes at 1846.9 and its child at 1798.4, so the sort itself added about **48 ms** (2.6%). Not the problem, despite being the top line.

**Go one level down.** The Nested Loop finishes at 1798.4 and its scan child at 1602.1, so the loop and inner scans add about 196 ms. The inner Index Scan ran 3,120 times at about 0.05 ms, roughly 156 ms, already on the primary key. The only lever there is fewer executions.
**Find the dominant node.** The `Seq Scan on visits` is **1602.1 ms, 87% of the query**. `Rows Removed by Filter: 2396880` is the smoking gun: it read 2.4 million rows to keep 3,120.
**Compute selectivity before prescribing.** 3,120 / 2,400,000 = **0.13%**: a highly selective predicate on a large table, exactly where an index wins.

learningExperiences.title: N+1: the pattern where every query is fast

contentBlocks.content:
## Lecture objectives

- Detect an N+1 pattern from a query log or trace.
- Restructure an access path so query count is bounded by the schema rather than by result size.
- Explain why eager-loading everything isn't the fix, and why the pattern isn't specific to ORMs.

## The shape of the problem

**N+1** is an access pattern that fetches a collection of N items with one query, then issues one more query per item for related data: N + 1 round trips where two would do. Here is the clinic's owner directory:

contentBlocks.caption: Nothing here is ugly. It reads well, the inner query uses an index, and each execution takes about 0.9 ms. That is the trap.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why "each query is fast" is no defense

The cost is **round trips**, not per-query duration. Each query pays driver serialization, network latency to the database, parse and plan lookup, execution, result serialization and latency back. Execution is often the smallest part.

With 200 owners in Reno and a 1.2 ms round trip, the page spends **240 ms in pure latency** before the database does meaningful work. No index removes this. Indexing `pets.owner_id` harder makes each query 0.8 ms instead of 0.9 and saves 20 ms out of 240. That is Section 1's `bottleneck-localization-m2` in a new costume: per-query time looked fine, so nobody computed share of total.

## How to detect it

1. **Query log:** a burst of identical SQL differing only in a bound parameter. The same statement twenty times in a row is N+1.
2. **Trace view:** a long stripe of short, uniform spans; visually unmistakable.
3. **Query-count assertion in tests:** assert that rendering the page issues a *bounded* number of queries. This catches it before it ships, and it is exactly how the code challenge below is checked.

## The fix: bounded, not maximal

Collect the IDs and issue **one** second query (`WHERE owner_id IN (...)`), then group the results in memory. Two queries whether Reno has 12 owners or 1,200. The defining property: **query count bounded by the schema, not by n.**

## It is not an ORM problem

Replace the database with an internal service and the pattern is identical and worse: `for a in appointments: a["pet"] = pets_api.get(a["pet_id"])`. The remedy is the same (a batch endpoint such as `pets_api.get_many(ids)`), but each round trip is now 15 to 40 ms instead of 1.2. ORMs get the blame because they hide relationship traversal, but the pattern belongs to the access path. Any loop containing a network call is a candidate, and so is a correlated subquery run once per row.

## An analogy

N+1 is a shopper who drives to the store, buys one item, drives home, checks the list, and drives back for the next item. Each trip is short, and a faster car (an index) makes each trip a little shorter, but the problem is the number of trips. The fix is to read the whole list first and buy everything in one trip. The opposite mistake, eager-loading everything, is buying the entire store to be safe.

## Summary

- N+1 costs round trips; per-query speed is no defense, and no index removes latency count.
- Detect it by repeated identical SQL, stripes of uniform spans, or query-count assertions in tests.
- Fix it by collecting IDs and issuing one batched query: constant query count in n.
- Eager-loading everything trades N round trips for one over-fetching join and is often slower.
- The pattern applies to service calls and per-row subqueries too.

workedExamples.title: Why "just eager-load everything" makes it worse
workedExamples.problem: Having learned N+1 is bad, an engineer configures the ORM to eager-load every association on owners: pets, each pet's visits, and each visit's invoice lines. The directory page shows owner name, city and pet names for 200 owners.
steps: **Count the rows produced.** 200 owners × ~1.5 pets = 300 pets. Each pet averages 39 visits: 11,700 visits. Each visit has ~3 invoice lines: **35,100 rows**.

**Account for join duplication.** Flattened into one result, each owner's name, city and pet attributes repeat on every one of the 35,100 rows. A 40-character city string alone becomes about 1.4 MB of redundant transfer.
**Measure what the page uses.** It renders owner name, city and pet names: zero visit data, zero invoice lines.
**Compare.** N+1 version: 201 queries, ~240 ms, ~300 useful rows. Eager-everything: 1 query, ~890 ms, 35,100 rows of which ~300 are used. The "fix" is **3.7× slower** than the bug.
**Apply the correct rule.** Load what this view renders, in a bounded number of queries. For this page, exactly two.
workedExamples.conclusion: The target is *bounded* loading, not *maximal* loading: query count constant in n, columns determined by the view.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. The resource being consumed is round trips; bounding the count removes them.
Indexing trims execution but leaves 240 ms of round-trip latency.
Indiscriminate eager loading over-fetches; in the worked example it was 3.7× slower than the bug.
That the tooling can't see it is why the pattern survives; the aggregate cost is what matters.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Count round trips × latency to price N+1. Batch the second query by ID so the count stays at two however long the list grows.

No. N+1 only happens with ORMs and SQL.
No, because HTTP calls can be cached.
Only if each call is slower than 100 ms.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. N+1 is a property of the access path, not the tool.
Any loop with a network call per item is N+1, and HTTP round trips are 10–30× more expensive than database ones.
Caching might hide some calls on hits, but the pattern and its cost on misses remain.

learningExperiences.title: Designing an index you can justify

contentBlocks.content:
## Lecture objectives

- Choose index columns and their order for a stated workload, justified by selectivity and prefix rules.
- Predict which queries a composite index can serve using the leftmost-prefix rule.
- State the write-path and storage cost an index incurs.

## Key terms

- **Selectivity:** the fraction of rows a predicate matches. `clinic_id = 7` matching 3,120 of 2.4 million rows (0.13%) is highly selective; `species = 'dog'` matching 58% of pets is not.
- **Composite index:** an index on an ordered list of columns, such as `(clinic_id, visit_date)`. The order is the whole design decision.
- **Leftmost-prefix rule:** a composite on `(a, b, c)` can serve predicates on `a`, `a, b`, and `a, b, c`, but generally not `b` alone or `c` alone. Entries are sorted by `a` first, so without a constraint on `a` there is no contiguous range to walk.
- **Covering index:** an index containing every column a query needs, so the database answers from the index alone (an index-only scan).
- **Write amplification:** the extra writes every index adds to each insert, update and delete.

rows: `clinic_id = ? AND visit_date >= ? AND visit_date < ?` ordered by `visit_date`
contentBlocks.caption: The `visits` workload (2.4 million rows, about 900 inserts a day).

contentBlocks.content:
## The failure mode this prevents

"Index every column in a WHERE clause" would give `visits` six single-column indexes. The planner would use one or two. Every insert would pay for all six, bulk loads would slow by multiples, storage would roughly double, and in the worst case the planner, offered several mediocre options, would pick a bad one. Over-indexing does its damage on the write path, which is exactly where a team measuring page loads won't notice.

## Misconception check: "column order doesn't matter"

This is `index-design-m2`. `(visit_date, clinic_id)` and `(clinic_id, visit_date)` contain the same columns and serve very different queries. For Q1, the first forces a walk through every September visit in all 40 clinics, checking each for clinic 7: about 40× more index entries read.

## Summary

- Order composite columns equality first, then range; columns after a range predicate stop narrowing.
- Leftmost-prefix rule: `(a, b)` serves `a` and `a, b`, not `b` alone.
- A covering index avoids table lookups at the cost of a wider index and more write work.
- Justify each index as read benefit × frequency against write cost × write rate.
- Several single-column indexes rarely substitute for one well-ordered composite.

workedExamples.title: Indexing the appointment list
workedExamples.problem: Design indexes for the three-query `visits` workload in the table above, and state the cost you accept.
steps: **Order columns: equality first, then range.** Q1 has equality on `clinic_id` and a range on `visit_date`. `(clinic_id, visit_date)` jumps to clinic 7 and walks a contiguous date range. The reverse walks every September visit across all 40 clinics: about 40× more entries.

**Check the prefix rule against the rest of the workload.** `(clinic_id, visit_date)` serves Q1 fully. It can't serve Q2 (`pet_id` isn't a prefix). It serves Q3 only by scanning the whole index, which is acceptable at 30 runs a month.
**Decide whether Q2 earns its own index.** 600/day is real traffic, `pet_id` is highly selective (~39 of 2.4 million rows, 0.0016%), and the first index can't help. Yes: `(pet_id, visit_date)`.

**Consider covering.** Q1 reads `pet_id`, `visit_date` and `cost_cents`. Extending to cover them (or an INCLUDE clause where supported) allows an index-only scan and skips 3,120 table lookups, at the price of a wider index. At 4,000 reads a day against ~900 inserts a day, reads dominate: take it.
**Reject what the workload doesn't support.** No index on `cost_cents` (nothing filters on it). No index on `clinic_id` alone (a redundant prefix of the composite).
**State the cost.** Two indexes on `visits`, one covering. Each insert now does three writes instead of one; updates to indexed columns update index entries too. At 900 inserts a day, negligible.
workedExamples.conclusion: Two indexes, with a stated read benefit (87% of a 1.8 s query removed, 4,000×/day) and a stated write cost (2 extra index writes per insert at 900/day). Benefit, frequency and cost in one sentence is what separates index *design* from index *accumulation*.

fadedVariant.problem: A pharmacy prescriptions table (5 million rows, ~20,000 inserts/day). Hot query: `WHERE store_id = ? AND status = 'ready' AND ready_at >= ?` (~50,000/day). A colleague proposes three single-column indexes on `store_id`, `status` and `ready_at`.
givenSteps: `status = 'ready'` is an equality predicate; `ready_at >= ?` is a range.
blankedStepPrompts: Propose one composite index and give its column order.
Why is the colleague's proposal worse?
State the write-cost sentence.
blankedStepAnswers: `(store_id, status, ready_at)`: both equality columns first, then the range column last.
Three single-column indexes triple the write cost, and the planner can use at most one or two of them, each far less selective than the composite.
One extra index write per insert at ~20,000 inserts/day, justified by serving ~50,000 reads/day with a narrow range scan.

options: WHERE clinic_id = 7 AND visit_date >= '2026-09-01'
WHERE visit_date >= '2026-09-01' alone
WHERE cost_cents > 20000
Any of them equally, since a composite index covers each column independently.

Entries are ordered by clinic_id first, so a filter on visit_date alone has no contiguous range.
cost_cents is not in the index, so the index can't narrow the search.
Column order is the whole design decision.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Walk the index left to right: each predicate must constrain the next column in order. Once you hit a column with no predicate, or pass a range, narrowing stops.
